passages.t: A leper made clean by a touch
passages.happening:
Jesus comes down from the mountain where he has been teaching, and large crowds follow him. A man with leprosy comes and kneels in front of him. “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.”

Jesus reaches out his hand and touches the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!” At once the man is clean. Then Jesus tells him to say nothing to anyone, but to go and show himself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, “as a testimony to them” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Matthew puts this story straight after the Sermon on the Mount. The sermon showed the authority of Jesus' words. Chapters 8 and 9 now show the same authority in his deeds. Mark tells the same healing early in his Gospel (Mark 1:40-45), and Matthew tells it more briefly.

‘Leprosy’ in the Bible is not only the illness doctors now call Hansen's disease. The Hebrew word covered a range of skin diseases, and even mould on cloth and on the walls of a house (Leviticus 13 and 14). A person with it was unclean, which means unfit to come near God's sanctuary, and the Law said, “He must live alone in a place outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:46). He had to wear torn clothes and call out ‘Unclean, unclean’ so that people would keep away. To touch such a person was to become unclean yourself.

So the touch is the shock of the story. Jesus did not need to touch the man; in the next story he heals with a word from far away. He touched him anyway. And the uncleanness does not pass to Jesus. His cleanness passes to the man.

Then Jesus sends him to the priest. Leviticus 14 sets out what a priest did when a skin disease had healed: he went out to examine the person, and if the disease had healed, the offerings the Law required were made and the person was declared clean. Jesus has just said that he came not to abolish the Law (5:17). Here he keeps it. The man is to go back into the life of his people by the door the Law provided.
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament, curing leprosy was thought of as something only God could do. When a foreign king sent the army commander Naaman to be healed, the king of Israel tore his clothes and asked, “Am I God, killing and giving life, that this man expects me to cure a leper?” (2 Kings 5:7). When Miriam was struck with the disease, Aaron begged that she not be “like a stillborn infant” (Numbers 12:12).

So when Jesus says ‘I am willing’ and the man is clean, Matthew's first hearers would have caught the question underneath: who is this, who does what Israel's king said only God could do? Later, when John the Baptist asks from prison whether Jesus is the one to come, Jesus will say, among other signs, “the lepers are cleansed” (11:5).
passages.hard:
The leper was sure Jesus could heal him. He was not sure Jesus would. Many sick people today ask the same question, and some have prayed for healing that did not come.

It needs to be said plainly, here at the start of these healing stories, and it holds for every one of them. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul begged the Lord three times to take away his ‘thorn in the flesh’ and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). He left his friend Trophimus “sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20). He told Timothy to take a little wine for his “frequent ailments” (1 Timothy 5:23). None of these men are blamed. Faith is trust in a person, not a payment that buys a cure. Seeking a doctor is not a failure of faith either; Paul called his friend Luke “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14).
passages.asks: The man's question was not ‘Can you?’ but ‘Will you?’ Which do you find harder to believe about God? Notice that Jesus answered with a touch before he answered with a word. Ask who in your life has gone untouched, and what it would mean to come near.

passages.happening:
In Capernaum a centurion, an army officer, comes to Jesus and pleads for his servant, who lies at home paralyzed and in terrible pain. Jesus says, “I will go and heal him.”

The officer stops him. “Lord, I am not worthy to have You come under my roof. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.” He explains: he is a man under authority with soldiers under him. He tells one to go, and he goes.

Jesus is amazed. He tells the people following him that he has not found anyone in Israel with such great faith. Many will come from east and west and sit at the feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while ‘the sons of the kingdom’ will be thrown outside. Then he tells the officer, “Go! As you have believed, so will it be done for you.” The servant is healed at that very hour.
passages.hearers:
A centurion was an officer in charge of a company of soldiers, in theory a hundred men. Galilee was ruled at this time by Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, under Rome. Many scholars think this officer most likely served in Antipas's forces, which were organized in the Roman way, rather than in a Roman legion. Either way he was a Gentile, a non-Jew, and he stood for the power that ruled the land. Luke's telling of the story adds that Jewish elders spoke up for him, saying, “he loves our nation and has built our synagogue” (Luke 7:5).

A devout Jew did not normally go into a Gentile's house. Years later Peter says to another centurion, “You know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or visit him” (Acts 10:28). The officer seems to know this. He spares Jesus the problem and asks only for a word.

His reason comes from army life. Orders pass down a chain of command, and an order given is an order done. He sees that Jesus' word has that kind of reach over sickness. His humble words have been spoken in worship for centuries. Since 2011, English-speaking Catholics say before receiving communion, ‘Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed.’

The Greek word for his ‘servant’ (pais) can mean a child or a servant. Most translations say servant here; in Luke's Greek he is called a slave (Luke 7:2).
passages.ot:
The feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob draws on the prophets. Isaiah promised that “the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples” on his mountain, and that he “will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:6, 8). Psalm 107 speaks of the redeemed “gathered from the lands, from east and west, from north and south” (Psalm 107:3).

Some of these promises, like Isaiah 43:5, speak of God bringing Israel's own scattered people home ‘from the east’ and ‘from the west’. So some readers think Jesus means scattered Jews coming home as well as Gentiles. In Matthew, though, the saying comes straight after a Gentile's faith, and the Gospel ends with Jesus sending his followers to “make disciples of all nations” (28:19). Most readers hear both: Israel's promised feast, with the nations coming in.
passages.hard:
What does Jesus mean by “the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness”? Christians have sometimes read these verses as God turning away from the Jewish people and replacing them with Gentiles. That reading is wrong, and it has done real harm.

Look at who is speaking and who is at the feast. Jesus is a Jew speaking to Jews. Every one of his first disciples was a Jew. The guests of honour at the banquet are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The warning is against taking your place for granted because of who your family is. John the Baptist gave the same warning: “do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’” (3:9). The warning falls just as hard on Christians who assume their place because they grew up in church.

‘Weeping and gnashing of teeth’ is Matthew's strongest picture of being shut out. He uses the phrase six times (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30). It is a picture of grief and anger at being outside. It is meant to wake people up, not to tell anyone which people group is in or out.
passages.asks: The man Jesus praised for great faith was an officer of the army that ruled Jesus' land. He had power, and he knew it gave him no standing before Jesus. Ask where you assume a place with God because of your family, your church, or your record, and where you might learn faith from someone you did not expect to learn from.

passages.t: Peter's mother-in-law, and the servant who carries our diseases
passages.happening:
Jesus comes to Peter's house and sees Peter's mother-in-law in bed with a fever. He touches her hand, the fever leaves her, and she gets up and begins to serve him.

That evening people bring him many who are troubled by demons. He drives out the spirits with a word and heals all the sick. Matthew says this fulfilled what Isaiah had said: “He took on our infirmities and carried our diseases” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Peter was married. Paul later mentions that Peter, whom he calls Cephas, took “a believing wife” with him on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5). In Capernaum a house has been honoured as Peter's since early times. It lies under the ruins of a church built in the 400s, and the pilgrim Egeria was shown a house of Peter there in the late 300s. It cannot be proved to be his house, but it is one of the oldest Christian memories of a place in Galilee.

The woman ‘began to serve’. In that world serving a guest meant getting up, preparing food, and waiting on the table. It shows how complete the cure was: no long weakness after a fever. It also shows a woman who, once healed, spends her strength on Jesus.

Mark explains why the crowd came only ‘when evening came’: it was the Sabbath, the day of rest, which ended at sunset, and carrying a load was not allowed until then (Mark 1:21, 32). Matthew leaves the Sabbath out and keeps the healing.
passages.ot:
Verse 17 quotes Isaiah 53:4, from the song of the suffering servant. The Greek translation of the Old Testament that many Jews used had turned this line into a saying about sins. Matthew does not follow it. His wording keeps the sense of the Hebrew: sicknesses and pains. He wants the reader to see that when Jesus heals, he is taking up people's real bodily burdens.

The same song goes on: “But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). Matthew quotes only the line about sickness here, but a reader who keeps going in the Gospel will see where this carrying leads: to the cross.
passages.hard:
Does verse 17 mean that healing of the body is promised to believers now, because Jesus carried our diseases? Christians answer in different ways.

Some teach that healing is provided in the atonement. ‘Atonement’ means the way the death of Jesus puts people right with God. On this view, Jesus bore our sicknesses as well as our sins, and believers may ask for healing with confidence on that ground. Isaiah 53:4-5 and Matthew 8:17 are the main passages they cite. F. F. Bosworth's book Christ the Healer (1924), widely read in Pentecostal circles, taught this.

Others point out that Matthew applies Isaiah to what Jesus did during his ministry in Galilee, before the cross, as a sign that God's kingdom had come. On this view the cross is the ground of every healing, but the full healing of the body waits for the resurrection, when God will remove “death or mourning or crying or pain” (Revelation 21:4). Meanwhile believers “groan inwardly” as they wait for “the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). Many Christians hold something between the two: God still heals, and all healing flows from the cross, but not all healing comes now.

Whatever view one holds, this verse is not a promise of health and wealth to those with enough faith. As the note on verses 1 to 4 says, no one should be told that an illness is the result of weak faith.
passages.asks: Matthew sees Jesus as the servant who carries other people's weight. Name a burden you are carrying that you have never brought to him. And notice what the healed woman did first: she got up and served. Ask how the strength you have been given could be spent on someone else today.

passages.happening:
Seeing the crowd, Jesus gives orders to cross to the other side of the lake. A scribe, a teacher of the Law, comes up and says, “Teacher, I will follow You wherever You go.” Jesus answers, “Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.”

Another disciple says, “Lord, first let me go and bury my father.” Jesus replies, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”
passages.hearers:
This is the first time in Matthew that Jesus calls himself ‘the Son of Man’. It was his favourite way of speaking of himself. It can simply mean ‘a human being’, but it also points to Daniel's vision of “One like the Son of Man” who is given “dominion, glory, and kingship” over every nation (Daniel 7:13-14). The shock is in the contrast. The one Daniel saw receiving an everlasting kingdom has nowhere to sleep tonight.

Burying your father was one of the most sacred duties a Jewish son had. It was part of honouring your father and mother, the fifth of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:12). When the prophet Elijah called Elisha, Elisha asked, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you” (1 Kings 19:20), and he was allowed to. Jesus goes further than Elijah did, and his first hearers would have felt how hard the words were.

What exactly was the man asking? Readers differ. Some think his father had just died, and the burial would happen that day. Others point to a custom of the time called secondary burial. A body was laid in a family tomb, and later, after the flesh had decayed, the family gathered the bones into a small stone box called an ossuary. Byron McCane argued in the Harvard Theological Review (1990) that the man may have been asking to wait until that second burial was done. Still others think the father was still alive, and the man meant, ‘Let me wait until he dies.’ On any reading, Jesus claims a loyalty that comes before even the most honoured family duty.
passages.hard:
‘Let the dead bury their own dead’ is one of the hardest things Jesus said, and it should not be softened. Most readers take ‘the dead’ to mean people who are not following Jesus, who are dead to the life he brings: let them see to it. The call to follow him cannot wait.

But it is not contempt for family. In this same Gospel Jesus rebukes people who used religion as an excuse not to care for their parents, quoting the command “Honor your father and mother” (15:4-6). On the cross he made sure his mother would be cared for (John 19:26-27). He wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). These words were spoken to one man at one moment, about what comes first. They do not tell anyone to stay away from a parent's funeral or to abandon a parent who needs care. Caring for an aging or dying parent is part of obeying Jesus, not a rival to it.

If you are grieving a father or mother now, hear this clearly: grief is not disobedience. Jesus himself grieved.
passages.asks: The scribe offered to follow Jesus anywhere; Jesus told him what ‘anywhere’ might cost. The second man wanted to follow, but later. Ask which of the two sounds more like you. And ask honestly whether something you call a duty has become a way of saying ‘not yet’.

passages.happening:
Jesus gets into the boat, and his disciples follow him. Suddenly a violent storm comes up on the lake, and the waves cover the boat. Jesus is asleep.

The disciples wake him: “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” He says, “You of little faith,” and asks, “why are you so afraid?” Then he gets up and rebukes the winds and the sea, and everything is completely calm. The men are amazed. “What kind of man is this? Even the winds and the sea obey Him!”
passages.hearers:
The Sea of Galilee is a lake lying about 700 feet below sea level, ringed by hills. Cold air dropping from the heights can stir up sudden, violent storms, and the fishing boats of the time were small.

Matthew tells this story with a few small changes from Mark (Mark 4:35-41). He alone says that the disciples ‘followed’ Jesus into the boat, straight after a passage about what following costs. Following Jesus can lead into a storm. He calls the storm a seismos, a ‘shaking’, the word he uses elsewhere for earthquakes (24:7; 27:54; 28:2). And he puts the order differently. In Mark, Jesus calms the storm first and then asks, “Do you still have no faith?” In Matthew, he speaks to the disciples first, in the middle of the storm, and calls them ‘of little faith’.

‘Little faith’ is a word Matthew uses several times (6:30; 14:31; 16:8). It is not the same as no faith. They did the right thing: they went to Jesus and cried, ‘Lord, save us.’ Their fear showed that they had not yet grasped who was in the boat with them.
passages.ot:
The scene echoes Jonah. There a storm hit the ship, Jonah lay in “a deep sleep”, and the captain woke him, hoping “that we may not perish” (Jonah 1:5-6). Later in Matthew, Jesus says, “now One greater than Jonah is here” (12:41). Jonah was asleep because he was running from God. Jesus sleeps because he is at peace with his Father.

In the Old Testament, it is God who rules the sea. Psalm 107 tells of sailors in a storm who cried to the LORD, and “He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29). So the disciples' question, ‘What kind of man is this?’, has an answer that Matthew wants his readers to reach for themselves.
passages.hard:
Does this story promise that if we trust Jesus enough, he will always calm our storms? No. Many faithful people have gone through storms that did not stop, and some have died in them. Matthew's point is who Jesus is, and that his followers are not alone in the boat.

And ‘You of little faith’ is not a rebuke of anyone who lives with anxiety or panic. Jesus said it to people who had come to him for help, and then he helped them. Anxiety that will not lift is something many believers carry, and getting help for it from a doctor or counsellor is wise, not faithless.
passages.asks: Think of a storm you are in now. The disciples brought it to Jesus with little faith, and that was enough for them to be heard. Ask what it would look like to bring yours to him today, with whatever faith you have.

passages.happening:
On the other side of the lake, in the region of the Gadarenes, two men troubled by demons come out from the tombs to meet Jesus. They are so violent that no one can pass that way. They shout, “What do You want with us, Son of God?” and, “Have You come here to torture us before the appointed time?”

Some distance away a large herd of pigs is feeding. The demons beg Jesus to send them into the pigs. “Go!” He told them. The spirits come out and go into the pigs, and the whole herd rushes down the steep bank into the lake and dies in the water. The herdsmen run into the town and tell everyone what happened. The whole town comes out to meet Jesus, and when they see him they beg him to leave their region.
passages.hearers:
Mark tells this story at length (Mark 5:1-20), and the notes on Mark 5 explain much of what a first hearer would catch: the east side of the lake was mostly Gentile country; pigs were unclean under the Law (Leviticus 11:7); touching a grave made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16). Every detail says ‘unclean’, and Jesus walks into the middle of it.

The place name is a puzzle in all three Gospels, and old copies of each show scribes trying to fix it. In Matthew, the best early manuscripts, Codex Vaticanus among them, read ‘Gadarenes’, and modern Bibles follow them. Many later copies read ‘Gergesenes’, which is why the King James Version has that name here. Others read ‘Gerasenes’, the name in Mark and Luke. Gadara, at modern Umm Qais in Jordan, stood about six miles southeast of the lake, and many think its farmland reached the shore. Gerasa was about thirty miles away. In the 200s the scholar Origen pointed to a town called Gergesa on the shore itself. One likely answer is that each Gospel names the district after a different town: the nearby city, the best-known city of the region, or the village on the spot.

The demons ask whether Jesus has come to torture them ‘before the appointed time’. They know a day of judgment is coming for them. They do not expect it so soon.
passages.hard:
Mark and Luke tell of one man, whom Mark names Legion. Matthew tells of two. Do the Gospels contradict each other?

The difference is real, and readers explain it in different ways. An old explanation is that there were two men, and Mark and Luke tell only of the one who spoke or who was better known; they never say there was only one. Others notice that Matthew has pairs elsewhere too: two blind men in 9:27 and again at Jericho in 20:30, where Mark names one, Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46). Some think Matthew gives two because the Law required “two or three witnesses” to establish a matter (Deuteronomy 19:15). Others say the Gospels follow the habits of ancient biography, which allowed a writer to shorten, combine, and arrange stories without meaning to mislead. Skeptical readers see a plain contradiction. Readers who trust the Gospels differ over which explanation is best, and the point of the story is the same in all three: people held by forces no one could tame are set free by a word from Jesus.

Were these men possessed, or ill? Matthew tells of evil spirits. He also lists ‘the demon-possessed’ and ‘those having seizures’ as different needs (4:24), so the Gospel itself does not treat every illness as a demon. As the notes on Mark 5 say, most suffering of the mind is illness, to be met with medicine and care, and no one should treat every illness as a demon. These men were feared and left among the tombs. If you or someone you love is struggling in mind, or harming themselves, please reach out for real help now, to a doctor, a pastor, or a crisis line.
passages.asks: The town saw two of its own set free and a herd lost, and it asked Jesus to leave. Ask whether there is any part of your life where you would rather keep what you have than have Jesus come close. And ask who in your town has been left ‘among the tombs’, avoided and feared, and who might go to them.
